title: Spinoza
hook: a philosopher put under a ban by Amsterdam's Jewish community, argued about ever since

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amsterdam, where people rebuilt a faith they had nearly lost. Your line was new home, old faith. Today, a son of that same community who walked another way.

In a small rented room, a man bends over a wheel, grinding glass into lenses: turn, polish, check against the light. In the evenings he writes, slowly, in Latin, building an argument the way he builds a lens, one exact surface at a time. Behind him, in Amsterdam, is the synagogue where he once studied as a boy. He no longer goes there. He can't. His own community has formally cut him off. Today, his name.
screen: `A MAN GRINDING LENSES.` → `WRITING IN LATIN AT NIGHT.` → `CUT OFF FROM HIS COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: Baruch Spinoza grew up inside the Amsterdam community we met yesterday, the Portuguese Jews who had worked so hard to rebuild. He studied in its schools and knew its texts. As a young man he was placed under a ban by the community's leaders, and the ban's own text speaks of evil opinions and acts without naming them. His later books show the questions he asked: who wrote the Torah, whether God chooses and commands as a person does, whether scripture should be read like any other old book. The ban was a cherem. It cut him off: members were told not to speak with him, come near him, or read what he wrote. Remember who those leaders were: former secret Jews, newly rebuilt, under the eyes of a Christian city that had taken them in. Some historians think they feared his ideas put everyone at risk. Others think the ideas alone were enough. Spinoza did not join another religion. He lived quietly elsewhere in Holland and wrote that God and nature are one reality, and that the Bible should be studied with the same tools as any text. People have never stopped arguing about him. Some Jews see him as someone who left, and say the ban stands for good reason. Others claim him as a forerunner of modern Jewish thought, and have asked for the ban to be revisited. Some readers call him a man who denied God, while a German poet called him a God-intoxicated man. The same pages, read in opposite ways.
screen: `A SON OF THE AMSTERDAM COMMUNITY.` · `QUESTIONS THE LEADERS COULD NOT ACCEPT.` · `THE CHEREM: CUT OFF.` · `READ IN OPPOSITE WAYS.` · then, large: `ARGUED ABOUT EVER SINCE.`

segments.voice: Pick one real question you carry, about God, about how to live, or about something you were taught. Without reaching for the answer someone gave you, or its opposite, ask: what do I actually know here, what am I guessing, and where does my thinking stop? Let the question stay open if it needs to; if you pray, you can bring it with you.
Spinoza. A philosopher raised in Amsterdam's Portuguese Jewish community, placed under a ban by its leaders, and argued about ever since. Today's word.
Your line: argued about ever since. The ban never named its reasons. See you tomorrow.
